question: What is Redwood Inference's complete end-to-end process for shipping an emergency serving-runtime hotfix to production (Hosted + Dedicated), including required approvals, checklists, rollout/rollback steps, and mandatory customer communications?
gold_answer:
To ship an emergency **serving-runtime hotfix** to production (Hosted + Dedicated), Redwood Inference follows this end-to-end process:

1) **Open the emergency change + record the minimum checklist** (in a Linear/Jira ticket and the incident timeline/thread): state the fix hypothesis, what's changing (code/config/infra), blast radius (Hosted regions, Dedicated clusters/customers, model families), risk assessment (security/data/perf), a **rollback plan with explicit triggers**, and who owns post-change monitoring; ensure an incident channel/thread exists with an identified IC.

2) **Get required approvals (no exceptions):** two-person approval from **(a) IC (or SRE on-call)** and **(b) the serving-runtime Service Owner (or delegate)**, recorded in PR review/incident thread/change record. Add scenario-based approvals as applicable: **Security on-call** (security/exploit), **Product on-call/PM** (customer-visible behavior changes), and **Customer Success Escalation Manager (CSEM)** when Dedicated/customer maintenance coordination is required.

3) **Prepare the hotfix PR (Serving Runtime Hotfix Runbook):** cut `hotfix/runtime-<YYYYMMDD>-<short-issue>`, cherry-pick only the minimal fix, update the Runtime Hotfixes changelog, open a PR (prefer release branch), and obtain emergency reviews from **runtime on-call + SRE on-call (or IC)**; include incident link, risk, rollback, and rollout owners.

4) **Build + supply-chain sign artifacts (mandatory):** run the approved hotfix build pipeline to produce the new runtime image in the production registry plus **SBOM** and **provenance attestation**, and **verify cosign signatures/attestations before rollout**; image signing cannot be skipped (SBOM delay is only allowed with Security on-call approval and must be attached within 4 hours).

5) **Validate before rollout (minimum required even in Sev-1):** run unit tests for the affected module, one perf canary for a representative model, and a stress test matching the incident pattern; record results in the PR confirming error-rate improvement, **no >10% p95 regression** (same workload), and no increase in OOM/GPU reset counters.

6) **Post rollout notes to the incident channel:** new runtime image tag, expected rollout impact (restarts/brief resets), the **canary target**, and **rollback criteria** (metrics + customer symptom). A canary is required unless explicitly waived by IC (with rationale recorded).

7) **Roll out to Hosted (Platform/SRE; Hosted Rollout + Rollback Procedure):** announce rollout start + tag; set `runtime_image_tag=<new-tag>` and sync via ArgoCD (`hosted-runtime`). Roll out in order **us-west-2a canary (10%) → us-west-2 (50%) → us-east-1 (50%) → eu-central-1 (50%) → global**, monitoring each step for at least 15 minutes (success rate, p95 for top routes, GPU OOM, router fallback, error-budget burn). **Rollback immediately** by reverting to the last-known-good tag and ArgoCD syncing if 5xx/stream aborts persist >5 min, OOM spikes >2× baseline, p95 regresses >20% for >10 min, crash loops appear, or customer reports correlate with rollout start; announce rollback and next steps in the incident channel.

8) **Roll out to Dedicated (Infra + CSEM; Dedicated Cluster Hotfix Rollout Notes):** collect required inputs (customer/cluster ID, current/target tags, expected restart impact, rollback tag, scope), obtain approvals (**IC/SRE + Dedicated service owner + CSEM sign-off on messaging**), and **communicate to customers** (unless IC explicitly waives due to active outage): state brief interruption risk, provide a rollout window, and describe rollback criteria in plain language. Canary one Dedicated cluster first (prefer internal dogfood/lowest-traffic with CSEM approval) and validate ~30 minutes (success rate, p95, OOM, restart frequency, customer health checks); then schedule remaining clusters, rolling **no more than 3 in parallel unless IC approves**. Per cluster: confirm comms sent, update Helm `runtime_image_tag`, ArgoCD sync `dedicated-<cluster-id>-runtime`, watch for CrashLoopBackOff, run customer smoke checks (chat/embeddings/streaming). If rollback triggers hit, revert the tag, restart if needed, and **notify the customer immediately** (CSEM).

9) **Mandatory Sev-1 customer communications (Status Page + Customer Notifications):** IC owns accuracy/cadence; CSEM owns direct enterprise/Dedicated outreach; initial acknowledgment **within 10 minutes**, updates **every 30 minutes** while impact continues, and a resolution message **within 15 minutes** of confirmed mitigation. Each update must include customer symptoms, affected surfaces (regions/clusters/models), mitigation steps, ETA with confidence level, and any workarounds; provide a post-incident summary within **1 business day** (required for enterprise).

10) **Post-change closeout:** update the incident timeline with start/change/outcome, record cluster/region outcomes, and within **2 business days** complete incident follow-up (what changed and why it worked), document any release-process deviations/corrective actions, remove temporary flags/throttles (with owner + deadline), and create a task to promote the hotfix into the next regular release.
answer_facts: An emergency serving-runtime hotfix requires opening an emergency change ticket and recording a minimum checklist: fix hypothesis, what is changing (code/config/infra), blast radius (Hosted regions and Dedicated clusters/customers), risk assessment (security/data/perf), an explicit rollback plan with triggers, and a named owner for post-change monitoring, with an incident channel/thread and identified incident commander (IC).

Required approvals for an emergency serving-runtime hotfix are two-person approval from (a) the IC or SRE on-call and (b) the serving-runtime Service Owner (or delegate), recorded in the PR review or incident thread/change record.

Additional scenario-based approvals apply: Security on-call for security or exploit risk, Product on-call or PM for customer-visible behavior changes, and a Customer Success Escalation Manager (CSEM) when Dedicated or customer maintenance coordination is required.

The hotfix PR process includes cutting a hotfix branch, cherry-picking only the minimal fix, updating the runtime hotfixes changelog, and opening a PR (prefer the release branch) that includes incident link, risk, rollback plan, and rollout owners, with emergency reviews from runtime on-call and SRE on-call (or IC).

Before rollout, the hotfix build must produce a new runtime image in the production registry along with SBOM and provenance attestation, and cosign signatures/attestations must be verified; image signing cannot be skipped, and any SBOM delay requires Security on-call approval and must be attached within 4 hours.

Minimum pre-rollout validation is required even in Sev-1: unit tests for the affected module, a performance canary for a representative model, and a stress test matching the incident pattern, with results recorded (including error-rate improvement, no more than 10 percent p95 regression on the same workload, and no increase in OOM/GPU reset counters).

Before executing rollout steps, the incident channel must be updated with the new runtime image tag, expected rollout impact (restarts/brief resets), the canary target, and rollback criteria; a canary is required unless explicitly waived by the IC with rationale recorded.

Hosted rollout is executed by Platform/SRE by setting runtime_image_tag to the new tag and syncing via ArgoCD for hosted-runtime, with rollout in order: us-west-2a canary (10 percent), then us-west-2 (50 percent), us-east-1 (50 percent), eu-central-1 (50 percent), then global.
Hosted rollout requires monitoring each step for at least 15 minutes using metrics including success rate, p95 for top routes, GPU OOM, router fallback, and error-budget burn.
Hosted rollback is performed by reverting to the last-known-good tag and ArgoCD syncing if any rollback trigger occurs, and the rollback plus next steps must be announced in the incident channel.

Hosted rollback triggers include: 5xx or stream aborts persisting more than 5 minutes, OOM spikes more than 2x baseline, p95 latency regressing more than 20 percent for more than 10 minutes, crash loops, or customer reports correlating with rollout start.

Dedicated rollout is executed by Infra with CSEM involvement, after collecting required inputs (customer/cluster ID, current/target tags, expected restart impact, rollback tag, and scope) and obtaining approvals from IC/SRE, the Dedicated service owner, and CSEM sign-off on customer messaging.
For Dedicated, customers must be communicated to (unless the IC explicitly waives due to active outage), including brief interruption risk, a rollout window, and rollback criteria in plain language.

Dedicated rollout must canary one cluster first (prefer internal dogfood or lowest-traffic with CSEM approval) and validate for about 30 minutes using metrics including success rate, p95, OOM, restart frequency, and customer health checks.
After Dedicated canary validation, remaining clusters are scheduled with no more than 3 clusters in parallel unless the IC approves more.

Per Dedicated cluster, execution includes confirming customer communications were sent, updating Helm runtime_image_tag, ArgoCD syncing dedicated-<cluster-id>-runtime, monitoring for CrashLoopBackOff, and running customer smoke checks (chat/embeddings/streaming).
If Dedicated rollback triggers are hit, the tag is reverted (and restarted if needed) and the customer must be notified immediately by CSEM.
Mandatory Sev-1 customer communications include use of a Status Page and customer notifications, with the IC owning accuracy and cadence and the CSEM owning direct enterprise/Dedicated outreach.

Sev-1 communications timing requirements are: initial acknowledgment within 10 minutes, updates every 30 minutes while impact continues, and a resolution message within 15 minutes of confirmed mitigation.
Each Sev-1 customer update must include customer symptoms, affected surfaces (regions/clusters/models), mitigation steps, ETA with confidence level, and any workarounds.
A post-incident summary is required within 1 business day for enterprise customers.

question: What is Redwood Inference's full "emergency production change" process for the serving runtime (Hosted API)-including required prechecks, approvals, rollout steps, customer comms, monitoring, and rollback?
gold_answer:
Redwood Inference's emergency production change (EPC) process for the Hosted API serving runtime is:

1) Confirm an EPC is permitted and start incident coordination
- EPC is permitted only if at least one is true:
  a) active Sev1/Sev2 incident needing mitigation
  b) credible imminent outage within hours (capacity exhaustion, crash-loop, widespread 5xx, auth outage)
  c) security vulnerability requiring immediate remediation
- If there is confirmed or likely customer impact: declare Sev1/Sev2, create the incident Slack channel, assign IC, Ops, Comms, and SME, and set cadence (default 15 minutes internal, 30 minutes external if impacted).

2) Required prechecks (do not skip)
1. Confirm customer impact and blast radius (regions, tiers, routes, top customers).
2. Confirm rollback path (last-known-good build/tag and the exact way to redeploy it; confirm the tag exists in the registry and the deploy tool can select it).
3. Confirm monitoring is available for: request success rate and 5xx by region, p95 latency, and runtime crash-loop/health (restarts).
4. Confirm customer comms plan: status page plan plus Support/CS brief per comms playbook.

3) Required approvals (role-based; can be in Slack but must be copied into the EPC record)
Minimum two-person approval before production impact:
- Hosted API serving runtime mitigation (hotfix, config, rollback):
  Approver 1: Incident Commander (IC) or Primary SRE Oncall (if no IC is declared)
  Approver 2: Serving Runtime Eng Oncall or Runtime EM
- Security fixes:
  Security Oncall plus IC/Primary Oncall (and follow Security IR process)
Additional escalation approvals:
- Risk tiers (emergency guardrails):
  Tier 0: rollback, disable flag, low-risk traffic shift within same model family
  Tier 1: runtime config changes affecting batching/caching limits
  Tier 2: scheduler/kernels or default kernel selection changes; requires explicit Runtime EM approval in addition to IC/SRE
  Tier 3: request semantics, auth, billing, or cross-region routing; requires VP Engineering (or delegate) unless pure rollback
- If the mitigation changes customer-visible behavior (responses/routing/model selection, token limits, throttling): Product oncall (or responsible PM) approval is required by the Emergency Change Policy v3.

4) Open required dashboards before changing anything (and keep them open through rollout)
Required dashboards/metrics:
- Hosted API request success rate (2xx/4xx/5xx) by region
- Runtime latency p50/p95/p99 and time-to-first-token (TTFT)
- Runtime crash-loop rate / container restarts
- GPU utilization and queue depth
- Error taxonomy: top runtime error codes (oom, kv_cache_eviction, stream_disconnect)
Guardrails during active Sev1:
- One change in flight per region at a time
- Each change must have a named owner and a named verifier
- Expand only after verifier states gate metrics are improving or flat
Error budget constraint:
- If Hosted API SLO error budget burn is above 2x normal (week-to-date): default to Tier 0 mitigations, require a canary of at least 10 minutes before expanding, and explicitly reconfirm rollback readiness (tag plus command).

5) Choose the safest mitigation first (stabilize first, then optimize)
Decision order:
1. If a regression started after a known deploy and rollback is available: rollback is preferred.
2. If rollback is not available or does not address the issue: apply a mitigation (disable experimental scheduler flags, reduce max tokens, adjust batch limits, reduce concurrent streams per pod, force conservative kernel selection, temporarily lower max output tokens for affected routes).
3. If the issue is correctness/security: do a minimal-diff hotfix with targeted rollout (avoid refactors).

6) Execute the change with controlled rollout steps and mandatory verification gates

A) Emergency rollback (serving runtime)
Use when rollback triggers are met or a mitigation will not be available quickly (for example, within ~30 minutes).
Common rollback triggers include:
- TTFT p95 regression > 30% in 2+ regions for 10+ minutes
- runtime-attributed error rate > 2% on generation routes (5xx, timeouts, OOM)
- repeated GPU OOM or kernel crash loops attributable to the new runtime build
Procedure:
1. Freeze rollout: pause any in-progress progressive delivery and ensure nothing auto-advances.
2. Capture in the incident channel before execution: current runtime release id, intended rollback target, blast radius, primary symptom, and confirmation that the prior release was known-good (at least 24 hours stable in prod if possible).
3. Roll back using deployment tooling to pin runtime_image_tag to the last-known-good tag, then roll back cohorts in a controlled order:
- If only a canary cohort exists: roll back the non-critical/unaffected region cohort first (if applicable), then the remaining canary cohort, then all regions currently on the bad release.
4. Verify after each region/cohort completes before proceeding:
- 5xx returns to baseline
- TTFT and p95 latency recover (no new sustained regression)
- restarts trend down; no new crash-looping pods
- GPU utilization and queue depth return to expected; OOM counters normalize
5. Post in incident channel what changed, where, and observed effect; link the rollback job/config change.

B) Emergency hotfix (runtime patch release)
Hotfix build and validation requirements (must not be skipped):
- Artifact provenance: build from a known branch and pinned commit SHA.
- Run unit tests relevant to the touched area (or document and get approval for exceptions).
- Security scanning (SAST + dependency scan) must run unless Security Oncall explicitly approves bypass.
- Rollback plan must be written before deploy.
Supply-chain requirements for hotfix artifacts:
- Container image must be signed (cosign); image signing cannot be skipped.
- SBOM must be generated and uploaded (exception: only a temporary SBOM upload delay is allowed with Security Oncall approval; SBOM must still be generated and attached within 4 hours).
- Provenance attestation must be generated; artifacts must be stored in the production registry.
Minimum additional validation for runtime hotfixes (record results in the PR):
- Unit tests for affected module
- One perf-canary run for a representative model (e.g., Llama 3.1 70B)
- One stress test matching the incident-triggering pattern (sequence length and concurrency)
- Ensure p95 latency does not regress > 10% vs the previous runtime image for the same workload and no increase in OOM/GPU reset counters.
Deploy/rollout sequence (Hosted fleet default):
1. Announce in incident channel that rollout is starting and which tag is being deployed; include expected rollout impact (restarts/brief resets), canary target, and rollback criteria.
2. Canary first: us-west-2a at ~10% traffic; monitor for at least 15 minutes.
   Canary pass thresholds (Hosted rollout procedure):
   - No sustained error rate increase > 0.2% absolute
   - p95 latency not worse than +10% vs previous runtime
   - No new crash-looping pods
3. Expand progressively:
- us-west-2 at 50% traffic
- us-east-1 at 50% traffic
- eu-central-1 at 50% traffic
- then global (all regions)
4. Stop and rollback if any monitoring gate trips (serving runtime hotfix gates; use as stop/rollback criteria during expansion):
- error rate +0.3% absolute sustained for 5 minutes
- p95 latency +15% sustained for 10 minutes
- restart rate doubles for 10 minutes
- GPU OOM events increase > 20%
Also immediately roll back on hard triggers:
- elevated 5xx or stream aborts correlated with rollout expansion
- widespread stream disconnects increase
- crash-loop/OOM increases
- customer escalations spike tied to the rollout region

7) Customer communications (required when customer-visible or experience-changing)
When to post to the public status page:
- Sev1: always; for runtime incidents with confirmed impact, post within 15 minutes of declaration
- Sev2: post if user-visible and expected to last > 30 minutes or many customers are likely to notice
- Any time we deploy a mitigation that changes customer experience (rate limits, reduced max output tokens, traffic shifting, paused rollout/rollback)
Coordination rules:
- Comms Lead drafts; IC approves external wording before posting.
- Notify Support and Customer Success with an internal brief before posting (in #support and #customer-success), and pin it in the incident channel.
Comms content requirements:
- Include symptoms customers see, affected product surface (Hosted API), regions if known, what mitigation is underway (paused rollout, rolling back runtime, deploying config mitigation), and the next update time.
- Do not name specific customers, do not speculate root cause, do not commit to exact recovery times, and do not share internal-only tags/cluster names unless explicitly approved for a specific customer.
After mitigation:
- Post a Monitoring update once metrics are stable for 30 minutes.
- Post Resolved only after IC confirms exit criteria.

8) Ongoing monitoring, exit criteria, and rollback readiness
- Continuously monitor success rate, 5xx, p95 and TTFT, streaming disconnects, restarts/crash loops, GPU queue depth/utilization, and top runtime error codes.
- Keep rollback readiness throughout (last-known-good tag confirmed, deploy procedure/job ready).
- Incident exit criteria (Hosted): error rates and latency back to baseline and stable for 30 minutes, and support queue stabilizing (no new spike of related tickets).

9) Mandatory artifacts and post-change requirements
Within 24 hours of EPC completion, produce an EPC record (Confluence page or linked incident timeline) containing:
- what changed and why
- approvals (who, when)
- start/stop times
- links to incident record and incident channel
- deployment identifier (GitHub PR, release tag, or config change id)
- evidence of verification (dashboard permalinks/screenshots, metrics callouts, or logs)
Additional requirements:
- If under an incident: incident timeline must include exact deploy/config times and observed effects after each mitigation.
- If EPC introduced risk (skipped tests, behavior change, partial rollout): open a follow-up work item for proper fix/regression tests and removing temporary flags/throttles (owner and deadline).
- For serving runtime EPCs specifically: document the final runtime version and configuration and whether any feature flags were left enabled.
- For Sev1: postmortem required; for Sev2: incident review required if customer-visible or if an EPC was executed; track follow-ups in Linear.
answer_facts: An emergency production change (EPC) for the Hosted API serving runtime is permitted only if there is an active Sev1/Sev2 incident needing mitigation, a credible imminent outage within hours, or a security vulnerability requiring immediate remediation.

If there is confirmed or likely customer impact, a Sev1/Sev2 is declared, an incident Slack channel is created, incident roles are assigned (IC, Ops, Comms, SME), and an update cadence is set (default 15 minutes internal and 30 minutes external when impacted).
Required prechecks include confirming customer impact and blast radius (regions, tiers, routes, and top customers).
Required prechecks include confirming a rollback path by identifying a last-known-good build or tag and verifying the tag exists in the registry and can be selected by deployment tooling.
Required prechecks include confirming monitoring availability for success rate/5xx by region, p95 latency, and crash-loop/health via restarts.
Required prechecks include confirming a customer communications plan (status page plan plus Support/CS brief per the comms playbook).
Before any production-impacting runtime change, a minimum two-person approval is required and approvals can be in Slack but must be copied into the EPC record.
For Hosted API serving runtime mitigations (hotfix, config change, rollback), approvers are (1) IC or Primary SRE oncall if no IC is declared and (2) Serving Runtime Engineering oncall or Runtime EM.
For security fixes, approval requires Security oncall plus IC or Primary oncall and following the Security incident response process.
Emergency change risk tiers exist (Tier 0 to Tier 3) and higher tiers require additional escalation approvals beyond the basic two-person approval.
Tier 2 changes (scheduler/kernels or default kernel selection) require explicit Runtime EM approval in addition to IC/SRE approval.
Tier 3 changes (request semantics, auth, billing, or cross-region routing) require VP Engineering (or delegate) approval unless the change is a pure rollback.
If the mitigation changes customer-visible behavior (responses, routing, model selection, token limits, throttling), Product oncall or the responsible PM approval is required.

Before changing anything, required dashboards are opened and kept open through rollout, including request success rate by region, latency including TTFT, crash-loop/container restarts, GPU utilization/queue depth, and top runtime error codes.

During an active Sev1, guardrails include one change in flight per region at a time and each change having a named owner and a named verifier, expanding only after the verifier confirms gate metrics are improving or flat.

If Hosted API SLO error budget burn is above 2x normal week-to-date, the default is Tier 0 mitigations, a canary of at least 10 minutes is required before expanding, and rollback readiness is explicitly reconfirmed.
Mitigation selection prioritizes rollback when a regression began after a known deploy and rollback is available.

If rollback is not available or does not address the issue, mitigations may include disabling experimental scheduler flags, reducing max tokens, adjusting batch limits, reducing concurrent streams per pod, forcing conservative kernel selection, or temporarily lowering max output tokens for affected routes.
For correctness or security issues, the hotfix should be a minimal-diff patch with targeted rollout and refactors should be avoided.

Emergency rollback triggers include TTFT p95 regression greater than 30% in two or more regions for 10 or more minutes, runtime-attributed error rate greater than 2% on generation routes, or repeated GPU OOM or kernel crash loops attributable to the new runtime build.
Emergency rollback procedure includes freezing rollout (pausing progressive delivery and preventing auto-advance) before executing the rollback.

Before executing a rollback, the incident channel records the current runtime release id, rollback target, blast radius, primary symptom, and confirmation the prior release was known-good (ideally stable in prod for 24 hours).
Rollback is executed by pinning runtime_image_tag to the last-known-good tag and rolling back cohorts in a controlled order, verifying results after each region/cohort before proceeding.

Rollback verification gates include 5xx returning to baseline, TTFT/p95 latency recovering without sustained regression, restarts trending down with no new crash loops, and GPU utilization/queue depth and OOM counters returning to expected.

Emergency hotfix build requirements include artifact provenance from a known branch and pinned commit SHA, running relevant unit tests (or documenting and getting approval for exceptions), running security scanning unless Security oncall approves bypass, and writing a rollback plan before deploy.

Hotfix supply-chain requirements include signing the container image, generating and uploading an SBOM (with only limited delay allowed by Security oncall approval), generating provenance attestation, and storing artifacts in the production registry.

Minimum additional hotfix validation includes unit tests for the affected module, a performance canary run on a representative model, and a stress test matching the incident pattern; p95 latency must not regress more than 10% versus the previous runtime image and OOM/GPU reset counters must not increase.
Hotfix rollout sequence includes announcing rollout start in the incident channel with the tag, expected impact, canary target, and rollback criteria.

Hotfix rollout starts with a canary in us-west-2a at about 10% traffic monitored for at least 15 minutes, with pass thresholds of no sustained error rate increase above 0.2% absolute, p95 latency not worse than +10% vs previous, and no new crash-looping pods.
After canary, rollout expands progressively to us-west-2 at 50%, us-east-1 at 50%, eu-central-1 at 50%, then global.

During hotfix expansion, stop and rollback criteria include sustained error rate increase of +0.3% absolute for 5 minutes, p95 latency +15% for 10 minutes, restart rate doubling for 10 minutes, or GPU OOM events increasing by more than 20%, and immediate rollback for hard triggers like elevated 5xx/stream aborts correlated with expansion or widespread stream disconnects/crash loops/customer escalation spikes tied to the rollout region.

Customer communications are required when the issue is customer-visible or the mitigation changes customer experience (for example rate limits, reduced max output tokens, traffic shifting, paused rollout, or rollback).

For Sev1 incidents with confirmed impact, a public status page post is required within 15 minutes of declaration; for Sev2, post if user-visible and expected to last more than 30 minutes or many customers are likely to notice.
External communications are drafted by the Comms Lead and must be approved by the IC before posting, and Support and Customer Success must be notified with an internal brief before posting.

Status communications should include customer symptoms, affected surface (Hosted API), affected regions if known, what mitigation is underway, and the next update time, and should not name customers, speculate root cause, commit to exact recovery times, or share internal-only tags/cluster names without explicit approval.
After mitigation, a Monitoring update is posted once metrics are stable for 30 minutes, and Resolved is posted only after the IC confirms exit criteria.

Ongoing monitoring includes success rate and 5xx, p95 and TTFT, streaming disconnects, restarts/crash loops, GPU queue depth/utilization, and top runtime error codes, while maintaining rollback readiness (last-known-good tag and deploy procedure ready).
Incident exit criteria for Hosted include error rates and latency back to baseline and stable for 30 minutes and the support queue stabilizing without a new spike of related tickets.

Within 24 hours of EPC completion, an EPC record must be produced documenting what changed and why, approvals, start/stop times, links to incident record/channel, deployment identifier, and evidence of verification.

If an EPC involved skipped tests, behavior change, or partial rollout, a follow-up work item is required for a proper fix/regression tests and removal of temporary flags/throttles with an owner and deadline.
For serving runtime EPCs specifically, the final runtime version and configuration must be documented, including whether any feature flags were left enabled.
For Sev1, a postmortem is required; for Sev2, an incident review is required if customer-visible or if an EPC was executed, and follow-ups are tracked in Linear.
Status updates must not name customers, speculate on root cause, or promise exact recovery times.
